analysis.one_liner: Caps the federal office that enforces minimum wage and overtime laws, cutting wage-theft enforcement.
analysis.headline: The bill attracted 6 House Republicans, never received a hearing or vote, and died in committee when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would set a hard ceiling of $229 million on the Labor Department's Wage and Hour Division spending for fiscal 2024. That division is the agency that enforces federal minimum wage, overtime, and child labor rules and recovers back pay for workers who were shorted. The bill was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee the day it was introduced and never moved again; it received no hearing, no markup, and no vote before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers who violate wage and hour laws would benefit from a smaller enforcement agency: fewer investigators means fewer audits, fewer back-pay actions, and lower odds of being caught underpaying workers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Employers at risk of wage-law enforcement

how_it_helps.text: The bill would cap the Wage and Hour Division's Salaries and Expenses account for fiscal 2024 at $229 million, a hard ceiling on the budget of the agency that enforces federal minimum wage and overtime rules.
The bill was introduced by Rep. Andy Biggs with five cosponsors — Reps. Rosendale, Gaetz, Good of Virginia, Roy, and Crane — all Republicans.
As a standalone appropriations-approval bill, it could only take effect if Congress adopted it as part of the annual funding process, which it never did.

analysis.who_pays: Low-wage workers, especially those in sectors with frequent wage violations such as food service, retail, construction, and agriculture, would bear the cost through less vigorous enforcement of the pay they are legally owed.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers owed minimum wage or overtime

drawbacks.text: A hard dollar cap on an enforcement agency reduces its capacity to investigate complaints, no matter how many workers file them; the bill sets the ceiling with no accompanying plan to prioritize cases.

Supporters would argue the division's budget grew quickly in recent years and that a statutory cap is a legitimate way to restrain federal spending and rein in an aggressive enforcement agency; a cap does not defund the agency, it limits how much it can spend.
Because the bill sets a specific fiscal-2024 ceiling rather than a structural change, its practical effect would have been limited to a single year's funding fight.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost falls entirely on workers who depend on the Wage and Hour Division to recover unpaid wages, while the benefit accrues to employers who would face less scrutiny. There is no provision that offsets the loss of enforcement for ordinary workers. The bill was also poorly positioned to accomplish anything on its own: as a single-year funding limitation without an appropriation attached, it could only matter if folded into a larger spending bill, and it never was.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Andy Biggs introduced the bill on March 29, 2023, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
The committee took no further action on the bill; its entire action history consists of introduction and referral.
The bill ended with five cosponsors, all House Republicans, and no votes were ever recorded on it.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill died without any floor action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers who rely on federal wage and hour enforcement are no worse off, because the enforcement budget was never capped; employers hoping for less scrutiny did not get what they wanted. No one materially gained — the bill simply went nowhere.

industries.industry: Employers in wage-violation-prone sectors (food service, retail, construction, agriculture)
industries.note: A smaller Wage and Hour Division enforcement budget means fewer investigators to audit pay practices and recover back wages, lowering the cost to employers of underpaying workers. The industry's gain is directly workers' loss of legally owed pay.

industries.industry: Enforcement-side labor law practitioners (worker advocates and wage-recovery attorneys)
industries.note: Reduced agency enforcement capacity shifts more wage-recovery work to private lawsuits, which reach fewer workers and cost more per case.
